scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

With Diwali just a week away, it's a great time to focus on key priorities to create a warm, festive atmosphere before your relatives arrive. Here’s what I’d recommend prioritizing first: 1. **Clean and Declutter (Start Immediately)** Diwali begins with *Dhanteras*, and cleaning is a traditional and essential first step. A tidy space makes decorating easier and more joyful. Focus on high-traffic areas like the living room, entrance, and puja room. 2. **Plan Your Diya & Lighting Layout** Decide where you’ll place diyas and string lights—especially along the entrance, windows, balconies, and around the puja area. This helps you buy or prepare the right number of diyas and cords. 3. **Purchase or Prepare Diyas and Candles** Get your diyas (clay lamps), candles, and LED fairy lights early. If using real oil diyas, make sure you have enough wicks and oil. Consider a mix of traditional and battery-operated ones for safety and convenience. 4. **Decorate the Entrance First** The main door is the first thing guests see. Create a welcoming look with: - A fresh *rangoli* (even a simple sticker one works!) - Diyas on either side of the door - A festive toran (door hanging) 5. **Set Up the Puja Area** This is the spiritual heart of Diwali. Clean and decorate your altar with flowers, diyas, idols, and offerings. Make sure it’s ready before the main Lakshmi Puja day. 6. **Add Final Touches (2–3 Days Before)** - Hang fairy lights and lanterns - Place diyas around the house (windowsills, balconies, pathways) - Refresh rangoli daily if possible - Add cushions, drapes, or festive tableware **Pro Tip:** Do a little each day—this avoids last-minute stress and keeps the energy positive. By focusing on cleanliness, lighting, and the entrance/puja area first, you’ll create a beautiful, inviting home that’s ready to welcome your loved ones with warmth and light. Happy Diwali preparations! 🪔✨

prediction.raw: 1 You are **not** the asshole. Here’s why: While your delivery could have been more tactful—especially given the intern was younger and possibly more sensitive—the **core of your action was reasonable and justified**. - **Littering is littering**, even if it's "organic." Banana peels take weeks to decompose and do not "feed the animals" in an urban or semi-urban environment. In fact, they can attract pests like rodents and contribute to the very fly problem you mentioned. The presence of flies—bad enough to require an exterminator—makes this a legitimate hygiene and workplace concern. - The trash can was **only 25 feet away**. This wasn’t a case of someone struggling to find a bin; it was careless disposal of waste in a shared space. - You were defending a **shared environment**. The sidewalk is a communal area used by many people. Allowing litter to accumulate sets a bad precedent and can encourage further inconsiderate behavior. - Yes, your tone was sharp and likely came across as harsh—especially first thing in the morning—but you didn’t insult her, threaten her, or act unprofessionally beyond the blunt comment and gesture. You stood by a reasonable expectation: *don’t litter*. - The fact that her boss **laughed about it** and recognized the overreaction on the intern’s part confirms that, in the workplace context, your response wasn’t seen as truly inappropriate—just direct. Could you have said it more kindly? Sure. A simple “Hey, mind tossing that in the trash? We’ve been having issues with pests,” might have gone over more smoothly. But being direct isn’t the same as being wrong. **Bottom line:** You’re not the asshole. You upheld basic standards of cleanliness and responsibility. The intern overreacted, and her boss seemed to agree. Stand by your values—just maybe with a cup of coffee in hand next time. ☕🍌🗑️
